transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-07-09 14:00 PDT
- Duration: ~55 minutes
- Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (CTO, ClearBanking Labs), Priya Menon (SRE), Hannah Brooks (Product), Oliver Grant (DevOps)

Auto-generated summary (brief):
- Quick results review from last week's burst test; Redwood SE ran a 2-hr spike, saw eviction behavior around reserve buffer at 85% utilization.
- Discussed tuning autoscale policy: target headroom, reserve buffer, eviction thresholds, and fallback model routing during overload.
- Agreed next steps: updated autoscale spreadsheet, 4-hour dry-run, share SOC2/KMS notes, confirm SSO cadence.

Topics:
- Recent burst test results and anomalies
- Autoscale policy tuning (scale-up/down windows, headroom, reserve buffer)
- Eviction/evicton playbook (reserve buffer eviction, graceful degradation)
- Dedicated sizing vs hosted fallback during burst
- Security: KMS, audit logs, SSO/SAML for Private deployment
- Next steps & benchmarks to collect

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: Okay everyone, thanks for joining. we'll kick off — I think we have about 55 minutes. quick round robin, who we got?
[00:06] Marcus: Marcus here — CTO, hi.
[00:08] Priya: Priya — SRE.
[00:09] Hannah: Hannah, product.
[00:10] Oliver: Oliver, DevOps.
[00:12] Samir: Great. Lena from Redwood on the call as well. uh, quick agenda: review the burst run logs, tune autoscale policy, walk through eviction playbook, and set dry-run date. any additions?
[00:25] Marcus: No, that's perfect. we want to make sure the Dedicated pool isn't surprising us with sudden evictions during peak auctions, right.
[00:33] Lena: Yep. so fyi, last week's 2-hour spike — we ran a synthetic workload that mimics your peak ecom flows, and we saw that when utilization crossed ~85% our reserve buffer started to get reclaimed. a few notes: we observed KV cache thrash when models were swapped for fallback; there were about 12 eviction events in the 2-hr window.
[00:52] Priya: When you say "reserve buffer" are you referring to the readwood reserve, like the buffer that holds warm instances for fast scalings?
[00:59] Samir: Yeah, sorry that's Redwood Dedicated reserve buffer — sometimes transcript says readwood — it's the reserved headroom we keep to avoid cold starts.
[01:10] Oliver: The weird bit we saw was occasional 500s for a handful of requests, mostly during the model swap back to primary; timeline suggests a 300–600ms spike for a subset.
[01:22] Lena: Right, the swap path still needs an optimization — when fallback model routes in, the KV cache rehydration hits the disk path if the node doesn't have the latest cache. that added ~200–400ms per affected request.
[01:37] Hannah: Is that more an infra thing or model packing? like can we tinker with cache TTL or pre-warm logic?
[01:44] Lena: Both. you can increase the reserve buffer or pre-warm extra shards during known sales windows. also our runtime supports prefix caching and a warmup API call to pre-populate KV caches.
[01:55] Marcus: What's the recommended reserve buffer percent? we saw 85% triggered reclaims, is 20% headroom too big cost-wise?
[02:05] Samir: We usually recommend 15–25% depending on burstiness. for very spiky traffic, lean to 20%. smaller headroom reduces cost efficiency but gives safer tail latencies.
[02:20] Priya: Could we do dynamic headroom, like schedule higher reserve for 1 hour windows around the promo?
[02:27] Lena: Yes — our autoscale policy supports time-based overrides. you can have a baseline policy and then an override window with different reserve buffer and scale cooldowns.
[02:36] Marcus: Cool. we also wanted to talk eviction policies — what happens when the reserve buffer is exhausted?
[02:44] Samir: When reserve buffer is exhausted we have a tiered eviction: first we route lower-priority requests to a smaller quantized model variant, then we start reclaiming worker allocations from lower-priority routes, and finally we reject traffic if thresholds are hit. the default thresholds are conservative, but you can customize per-tenant.
[03:05] Oliver: Is model quantization safe for our e2e quality? last week we saw a small but measurable increase in hallucination for one prompt set in the test.
[03:15] Lena: Quantization can affect quality in edge cases. our Optimize team suggests using it for non-critical routes like metadata enrichment. for core transaction paths we prefer smaller model variants only as a last resort, and we can route to hosted fallback with a different cost tradeoff.
[03:30] Hannah: Hosted fallback meaning send to Redwood hosted API? will that leak data?
[03:36] Samir: For POC we can tie the fallback to a redwood-hosted endpoint that has PII redaction and retention controls. but yes you need to accept that hosting path has a different data residency profile — for ClearBanking Labs we flagged that as a concern so we'd prefer VPC private fallback or on-prem micro-fallback if possible.
[03:58] Marcus: So two questions: 1) will fallback to hosted be instant and cheap? 2) can we do a private fallback within our VPC?
[04:06] Lena: Hosted fallback is fast but implies egress and retention differences. Private fallback inside the VPC is supported with Redwood Private; it requires a control-plane peering and a small reserved pool. It is more operational work but meets your compliance.
[04:22] Priya: On the compliance note — can you re-send the KMS integration flow? last time the doc had a few gaps around key rotation and audit logs.
[04:31] Samir: Yeah I'll resend the KMS + minimal-privilege flow, and Lena will annotate the audit log retention fields.
[04:37] Lena: I'll include sample CloudTrail events and the path for HSM-backed keys.
[04:43] Oliver: Thanks. back to scaling: what's the scale-up/down cooldowns you suggest? we noticed oscillation in the trial where pool scaled up, then a quick scale-down and then thrash.
[04:54] Lena: We recommend asymmetric cooldowns: faster scale-up (30–60s) and slower scale-down (3–5 minutes) to avoid flapping. Also consider using sustained-utilization windows so transient spikes don't cause immediate scale-down.
[05:10] Marcus: For our traffic, which is spiky but has repeated pulses, maybe keep scale-down to 5 minutes.
[05:18] Samir: Makes sense. another lever is burst credit — you can specify a short-term burst budget where requests can draw additional capacity for X minutes, then it drains. this is good for promo bursts.
[05:30] Hannah: Are burst credits billed differently?
[05:33] Samir: They are accounted for in the cost model; think of it as ephemeral capacity charged at slightly higher premium, but it avoids long-term overprovision. I'll put numbers in the spreadsheet.
[05:43] Priya: On the eviction playbook doc side — can we get a runbook that maps status codes to run actions? e.g., 429 on primary -> route to fallback, 500 -> rehydrate caches, etc.
[05:54] Lena: We have a template. we'll tailor it: map a three-step escalation, runbook for SRE, and a manual rollback to previous model if quality degrades.
[06:04] Marcus: What about observability — we need token-level cost breakup and per-route latency p95/p99. are those available?
[06:12] Samir: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, plus per-route latency histograms and p95/p99. we'll provision read-only dashboards for your team.
[06:20] Oliver: Good. also network egress — we have strict cloud egress budgets, can we pin region affinity?
[06:27] Lena: Yes, you can pin region routing and we can also restrict fallbacks to the same region for egress control. region affinity is part of the routing policy.
[06:36] Hannah: Quick note — during last test we noticed occasional mis-attribution in the logs where user IDs were redacted inconsistently — might be transcriber or instrumentation bug.
[06:46] Lena: We'll double-check the telemetry pipeline; likely a log enrichment step ran before redaction in one path.
[06:52] Samir: Alright let's go into the proposed autoscale policy in the spreadsheet — Lena, do you want to walk through the key knobs?
[07:00] Lena: Sure. high-level: baseline target utilization 65%, reserve buffer 20% during promo windows (else 15%), scale-up threshold 75% with 45s window, scale-down threshold 50% with 5m cooldown. eviction threshold at 95% cluster utilization triggers fallback routing, then preemptible reclaim.
[07:24] Marcus: Why 65% baseline? is that for cost efficiency?
[07:27] Lena: Yes, 65% is a balance between throughput cost and tail latency; it minimizes idle GPU while keeping room for short bursts.
[07:33] Priya: How do we ensure the reserve buffer is not drained by internal housekeeping or maintenance tasks?
[07:39] Lena: We tag reserve buffer nodes and guard them via scheduler affinity; also the runtime will not schedule low-priority batch jobs on reserve nodes.
[07:48] Oliver: About quantized smaller models — can we pre-load them on warm nodes to avoid cache thrash?
[07:54] Lena: Yes pre-loading and using a small warming request stream reduces rehydration cost. we can add a pre-warm step in the playbook.
[08:02] Hannah: We had a question on data retention: do logs include prompts? we need prompt redaction for compliance.
[08:09] Samir: By default you can set prompt redaction on ingestion; the console will then store only token metadata. we can set different retention windows per environment.
[08:18] Marcus: Good. can we talk briefly about the 4-hour dry-run plan? what are success criteria?
[08:24] Samir: Success criteria proposed: no more than X% 5xx during burst (we'll set exact number with you), p99 below target SLA (you'll give us target), and evictions below Y events per hour. also no sustained increase in hallucination rate above baseline for core prompts.
[08:37] Marcus: Our product team will put together the prompt set and quality check script.
[08:41] Hannah: I'll do that — we'll run the replay tool against staging and flag regressions.
[08:45] Priya: For the dry-run we'll need a staging env that mirrors production KV sizes — can you confirm costs and provisioning lead time?
[08:51] Lena: Staging provisioning is ~48 hours if we need additional Dedicated nodes. cost is proportional to reserved capacity — I'll add a rough estimate.
[08:59] Oliver: If provisioning takes 48 hours, let's lock in the dry-run window now.
[09:02] Samir: proposal: July 20th 22:00 UTC for 4-hour window. does that work?
[09:08] Marcus: That should be okay — Marcus approves tentatively.
[09:10] Priya: Works for SRE as well.
[09:12] Samir: Great. action items we'll capture. quick Q from Oliver: can we set a soft-eviction level that routes only non-critical routes out?
[09:21] Lena: Yup—route priority mapping supports that. you can tag routes as critical, best-effort, or background and evict in that order.
[09:29] Oliver: Nice. competitor question — FastServeAI has a similar burst credit idea; how is Redwood different?
[09:36] Samir: Our difference is first-class KV cache rehyration and integrated fallback routing per-route, plus the Console's token-level cost plus the private deployment mode so you don't have to choose between compliance and performance.
[09:49] Marcus: Financial question — can you show the cost delta between 15% and 20% reserve?
[09:54] Samir: I'll add that to the spreadsheet — rough ballpark: 15% headroom ~5–8% lower monthly cost vs 20% but with higher tail risk. exact depends on tokens and inference time.
[10:07] Hannah: Are there any recommended A/B tests for quality when using quantized fallback?
[10:13] Lena: Yes run side-by-side with a sampling rate and instrument hallucination detection; Redwood has a quality regression harness you can plug in.
[10:21] Marcus: Okay any blockers on the security checklist?
[10:25] Priya: just need the KMS rotation details and SSO cert rotation window. once we have that we can sign the security addendum.
[10:33] Samir: noted, will send.
[10:36] Lena: One last ops note: we'll include a small script to replay eviction scenarios so you can exercise the fallback path without real traffic.
[10:45] Marcus: That's useful.
[10:47] Samir: Alright let's recap and confirm next steps.
[10:51] Hannah: Recap: Samir sends autoscale spreadsheet and cost delta; Lena runs 4-hour burst in staging and shares logs; Priya confirms SSO/KMS windows; we schedule dry-run July 20; product provides prompt set and quality tests.
[11:10] Samir: yep. any other questions?
[11:14] Marcus: none from me. thanks everyone.
[11:17] Samir: Thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invite and docs.
[11:20] (call ends)
